transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2025-05-16 16:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Noah (Redwood Product), Eleanor (Stratus), Diego (Stratus), Aisha (Stratus)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood walked through the model picklist workflow in the Console, showed how benchmarks and the compatibility matrix map to hardware profiles and routing policies. Discussion covered hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs for PCI-sensitive workloads, telemetry/audit logs, and a scoped bench sprint (pilot) to validate latency and per-token costs. Action items captured to share bench matrix, security artifacts, and to schedule pilot kickoff.

Topics:
- Console model picklist and shortlists
- Benchmarks and interpreting latency/cost profiles
- Compatibility matrix (kernels, quant, hardware)
- Routing/fallback policies and SLOs
- Private deployment / VPC / KMS concerns
- Pilot scope and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll run through a focused demo on the model picklist, how the bench sprint would work, and then map that back to your compliance constraints. did i get the agenda right?
[00:12] Eleanor Park: yes thanks, and quick note — our timeline is tight; we want a pilot within two weeks if possible because the payments compliance window is coming up.
[00:20] Maya Patel: okay great, we can scope that. quick real quick intros? i'm maya on the SE team, i usually own runtime mapping and kernels.
[00:29] Diego Ruiz: diego, platform engineer, i'll own the infra side — vpc, firewall rules, certs.
[00:34] Aisha Khan: aisha, security architecture. SOC2 and key management are our top priorities.
[00:40] Noah Rivera: i'm noah on product, i'll show the Console playbook and the Optimize recommendations later.

[00:52] Liam Chen: jumping in — first slide, very high level: model picklist in the Console shows curated opens, performance bands, and a compatibility matrix. the idea is you can short list models for your workload, then run bench sprints to collect real cost/latency numbers.
[01:10] Eleanor Park: curious — when you say compatibility matrix, does that include kernel-level support for quantized variants? we have to keep throughput high for realtime auth flows.
[01:20] Maya Patel: yes — the matrix maps model families to recommended kernel paths and quant profiles. e.g., gpt-ish open models can run in 4-bit quant with our optimized kernels, but we call that out because there are quality tradeoffs on some instruction-following tasks. sometimes the transcript will read "G P T-ish" in the auto text — apologies, but you'll see the details in the matrix.
[01:45] Liam Chen: also important, the matrix shows compatible hardware (A100, H100, custom infer accelerators), expected tail latency percentiles, and throughput at different batch sizes.

[02:10] Diego Ruiz: how do you measure tail latency? our SLO is 95th <= 220ms for single-turn auth.
[02:18] Maya Patel: we provide percentile metrics from bench runs and from live telemetry. for bench sprints we run representative prompts with your token distribution, measure p50/p90/p95, and give a cost per 1k tokens estimate. for your SLO of 220ms p95 we can flag models that meet that on the target hardware.

[02:45] Eleanor Park: and is that bench run done in hosted or on a dedicated pool? we need to know isolation and data residency for PCI.
[02:53] Liam Chen: great question — pilot options: hosted API (fastest signup) or Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) or Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). for PCI-sensitive flows we typically recommend Dedicated or Private so audit logs and KMS are under your control.
[03:12] Aisha Khan: can you walk through KMS integration? we use an HSM-backed KMS and rotate keys quarterly.
[03:20] Maya Patel: yes — Private supports customer KMS via standard KMS/HSM integrations; we record key IDs in audit logs. for Dedicated we offer customer-managed key options and full audit trails. we'll attach our SOC2 pack and KMS guide.

[03:45] Noah Rivera: switching to the Console — (screen-share) here's the picklist view. you can import a shortlist (CSV or via API) or use our scouting recommendations. each model card has: estimated latency band, quality signal from evals, and a compatibility row where you can expand to see kernel/quant/hardware notes.
[04:10] Liam Chen: note that the quality signal is from our eval runs and from your own bench if you upload reference prompts. we surface regressions and give A/B compare.

[04:28] Eleanor Park: is there a way to automatically route to a cheaper variant when load spikes but still preserve quality? we can't have auth failures but can tolerate slightly lower generation quality for less-sensitive responses.
[04:40] Maya Patel: yes — that's the routing and fallback policy. you can set a primary model and fallback to a cheaper quantized variant or a smaller model based on latency or cost thresholds. we also support region fallback and redundant pools to avoid outages.

[05:05] Diego Ruiz: does fallback preserve conversation state? our product needs KV cache to persist across the switch.
[05:12] Maya Patel: yep — we maintain KV cache compatibility for model variants when they're architecturally compatible. there are edge cases when crossing model families; we'll flag those in the compatibility matrix and in the rollout plan. sometimes the auto transcript mistranscribes "KV cache" to "KV cash" — ignore that.

[05:35] Liam Chen: demo continuing — zoom into Bench sprint flow. Step 1: share sample prompts & traffic mix. Step 2: Redwood runs head-to-head on selected model shortlist across hardware profiles. Step 3: we deliver a bench report with latency percentiles, cost per 1k tokens, and suggested runtime config (batch sizes, prefix cache, quant).
[06:00] Eleanor Park: how long does step 2 take?
[06:03] Maya Patel: typical bench sprint is 3–5 business days once we have prompts and traffic profile. if you want faster we'll prioritize likely candidates first.

[06:18] Lionel? [speaker label glitch] Noah Rivera: small note — the Optimize tab will give automated suggestions like "increase batching to 8 for this model on A100 to reduce per-token cost by 18%" or "enable prefix/KV cache for repeated context to drop token count by 12%".

[06:40] Diego Ruiz: for the pilot, do you need us to provision any infra?
[06:44] Liam Chen: for a Private pilot we need VPC peering details and a service account; for Dedicated we provide dedicated pools and a customer network configuration; hosted needs just an API key and sample dataset. since you're PCI-sensitive i'd recommend Dedicated to start.

[07:05] Aisha Khan: what about logs and retention? auditors want 1 year of request logs with token redaction.
[07:12] Maya Patel: we support configurable retention in Console. for Private/Dedicated we'll set retention policies and can offer token redaction at ingest. we'll include logging configuration in the security pack.

[07:31] Eleanor Park: okay, on success criteria — we'll measure: 1) p95 latency under 220ms for auth prompts, 2) cost per 1k tokens in line with our budget (target <$0.12/1k tokens for the auth path), and 3) no unacceptable regression in answer quality measured by our reference prompts.
[07:50] Liam Chen: great— we'll include those as pilot success metrics.

[08:00] Maya Patel: quick technical aside — some models benefit from kernel-level fused attention and custom CUDA kernels; our Console flags models that need specific kernel builds and whether we support quantized 4-bit inference. that often explains why a model's latency band can vary by 2–3x across hardware.

[08:30] Diego Ruiz: are runtime configs exportable? we want to version them in our infra repo.
[08:34] Noah Rivera: yes — configs and rollout policies are exportable via the API and can be checked into your repo. we also have a Terraform provider in beta.

[08:52] Eleanor Park: any red flags — like models that look cheap but have hallucination issues?
[08:58] Maya Patel: we flag quality signals — a model might be cost-efficient but show lower factuality on certain eval suites. part of the bench sprint is targeted evals on your domain prompts. we also support reranking or hybrid pipelines (embedding+retrieval + model) if that helps lower hallucination.

[09:20] Liam Chen: let's talk scope for the pilot bench sprint. recommended shortlist: 3 models — (1) high-quality open model, (2) mid-tier quantized variant, (3) small low-latency model for fallback. we run them on 2 hardware profiles (A100 and H100 or equivalent) and measure p50/p90/p95, tokens per second, and cost.
[09:46] Eleanor Park: sounds good. for prompts we'll provide 2000 auth prompts, 500 longer contextual prompts, and a traffic split.

[10:00] Maya Patel: perfect. we'll also run a lightweight live soak on hosted to gather telemetry if you agree. that helps validate tail latency in realistic conditions.

[10:12] Diego Ruiz: is there any impact to our existing rate limits or WAF?
[10:16] Liam Chen: no change to your WAF; for Dedicated/Private we respect your existing rate limiters. Redwood Console also provides per-route quota controls.

[10:30] Aisha Khan: on encryption in transit and at rest — TLS + customer KMS for at-rest keys is required. do you support our HSM vendor?
[10:38] Maya Patel: we integrate with multiple KMS/HSM vendors; we'll confirm compatibility in the security pack.

[10:50] Noah Rivera: a quick note on costs — bench report will include an estimated per-token cost and a suggested runtime config that often reduces cost by combining batching and prefix caching. Optimize will show expected savings.

[11:05] Eleanor Park: one more Q — if we choose Dedicated, can we still fall back to hosted in bursts?
[11:11] Liam Chen: yes — we support burst overflow to hosted capacity with data handling policies and fallbacks; you can configure whether overflow uses a scrubbed dataset or full context. for PCI you might prefer overflow disabled, but that's configurable.

[11:30] Diego Ruiz: what about SSO/role-based access? we need RBAC and SAML SSO.
[11:35] Maya Patel: Console supports SAML SSO and granular RBAC. we can create a role for bench viewers and separate roles for runtime operators.

[11:45] Liam Chen: final recap: we'll send the bench matrix template, security/SOC2 pack, and a pricing estimate. you'll provide prompt corpus and traffic profile. we'll target pilot kickoff the week of 2025-05-26.

[11:59] Eleanor Park: sounds good; good demo. please also include an example of a fallback policy in the docs.
[12:06] Liam Chen: will do. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
